reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Baran and Dawber's Diseases of the Nails
clinicalPearls: Koilonychia describes a thin, flattened or concave nail with everted edges, so that the plate is spoon-shaped and can theoretically hold a drop of water
It is classically linked to iron-deficiency anaemia and may accompany the dysphagia of Plummer-Vinson (Paterson-Kelly) syndrome
A gentle, self-limiting form is normal in many infants and young children and resolves as the nail thickens with age
Occupational and environmental softening, from prolonged contact with solvents, oils, or repeated wetting, is a recognised acquired cause
It can also occur with haemochromatosis, thyroid disease, and some hereditary nail disorders
Because iron deficiency is the most treatable systemic association, checking iron status is a sensible early step in unexplained adult cases
Management centres on correcting the underlying deficiency or disease and protecting the nails from softening chemicals and trauma
reference.pathophysiology: Koilonychia develops when the normal transverse and longitudinal curvature of the nail is lost or reversed, producing a flattened or upturned, concave plate. A thin, soft plate is more easily deformed by the ordinary pressures of daily use, and reduced availability of iron, which is required for the keratinisation and structural integrity of the nail, is thought to contribute in deficiency states. Softening from repeated exposure to water, solvents, or oils has a similar mechanical effect, while in infancy the nail is naturally thin and pliable, explaining the transient physiological form that corrects itself as the plate matures.
additionalDifferentials: Occupational or chemical softening of the nail
Lichen planus or psoriasis producing nail thinning
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and iron studies (ferritin, serum iron, transferrin saturation)
History of occupational and domestic exposure to solvents, oils, and wet work
Thyroid function tests where clinically indicated
Assessment for dysphagia and consideration of Plummer-Vinson syndrome
Iron overload screen (transferrin saturation, ferritin) if haemochromatosis suspected
Onychoscopy and examination of all nails to define the pattern and severity
redFlags: Koilonychia with dysphagia, suggesting Plummer-Vinson syndrome and possible upper oesophageal web
Persistent unexplained iron deficiency requiring investigation for occult blood loss
Associated systemic features of haemochromatosis such as skin pigmentation and joint disease
New adult-onset koilonychia without an obvious mechanical or occupational cause
reference.prognosis: The physiological form of childhood resolves spontaneously, and acquired koilonychia usually improves once the cause, particularly iron deficiency, is corrected, although the flattened nail only normalises gradually as new plate grows out.
pitfalls: Diagnosing pathological koilonychia in an infant when the finding is a normal transient variant
Treating the nail deformity without checking iron status in an adult
Missing an occult source of blood loss underlying the iron deficiency
Overlooking occupational chemical exposure as a reversible cause
references: Baran and Dawber's Diseases of the Nails and their Management
management: Identify and treat the underlying cause, with oral or intravenous iron replacement for iron-deficiency anaemia as the most treatable association
Investigate and manage other systemic associations, including venesection for haemochromatosis and correction of thyroid dysfunction
Assess for dysphagia and an oesophageal web and manage associated Plummer-Vinson syndrome
Reduce occupational and environmental nail softening by minimising contact with solvents, oils and repeated wetting, using protective gloves and emollients
Reassurance and observation for the physiological infantile form, which resolves as the nail plate thickens with age
Monitor gradual normalisation of the nail as new plate grows out once the cause is corrected
